slides.title: Your Challenge: Draft a Bill
slides.storyContext: MP Sharma asks Rajesh: 'What changes do YOU want? Draft a bill. What's the problem? What's your solution?'

points.label: Example problem
points.text: Schools don't have girl toilets. Girls drop out. Solution: pass law requiring all schools have separate girl toilets, water supply.

points.label: What to include
points.text: Problem statement. Proposed solution. Who implements? How funded? Timeline? Penalties for non-compliance?

points.label: Debate points
points.text: If you propose your bill in class, others will challenge: 'Cost too much?' 'Central government or state's job?' 'How to monitor?'

points.label: Reality check
points.text: Most bills require government funding or regulation. How will you pay? What agency executes? Realistic or fantasy?

example.problem: Draft a bill: All villages must have a government health clinic within 5 km.
example.solution: Problem: villagers die of treatable diseases because no clinic nearby. Solution: government establishes clinic with 2 staff, free medicines, every village >1,000 people. Funded by central budget (Health Ministry). Checked by state health department. Timeline: 5 years. Penalty: state loses federal health grant if noncompliant.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bills start with real problems. You identify what's wrong, propose a solution, design implementation, debate costs. Then Parliament votes.

slides.title: Ordinances: When Parliament Can't Wait
slides.storyContext: Minister Verma explains: 'Sometimes government can't wait for Parliament to debate for months. If there's an emergency (pandemic, disaster), PM can issue an Ordinance—an emergency law that takes effect immediately.'

points.label: What is an Ordinance?
points.text: A law issued by President on PM's advice when Parliament is not in session or too slow. Takes effect immediately.

points.label: Duration
points.text: Ordinance lasts 6 weeks after Parliament reconvenes. Must be converted to law (bill) within that time, or it expires.

points.label: Examples
points.text: COVID-19: Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Ordinance 2020 to expand hospital beds, oxygen supply. No time for 3-month bill process.

points.label: Danger
points.text: Can be misused. PM could issue Ordinance to override Parliament. Constitution limits it: only during emergency, and Parliament can reject.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ordinances are emergency laws PM issues when Parliament is unavailable. Used in crises but can be abused if not checked by Parliament.

slides.title: Parliamentary Privileges and Immunities
slides.storyContext: MP Sharma tells Rajesh: 'In Parliament, I have freedom of speech. I can criticize government, minister, even President. Can't be arrested for speech inside Parliament. This is parliamentary privilege.'

points.label: Parliamentary privilege
points.text: MPs have immunity from legal action for statements made in Parliament. Can't sue for defamation if you criticize someone there.

points.label: Why this protection?
points.text: Allows MPs to speak freely without fear of government silencing them. MPs represent people, must voice people's grievances without censorship.

points.label: Limits
points.text: Privilege doesn't cover statements outside Parliament (media, social media). Inside Parliament only.

points.label: Example
points.text: MP can say 'Minister X is corrupt' in Parliament. But if said on Twitter without proof, can be sued for defamation.

slides.inSimpleWords: MPs can speak freely in Parliament without fear of legal action. This freedom is necessary for democracy but doesn't extend outside Parliament.

slides.title: Public Interest Litigation: Citizens as Guardians
slides.storyContext: Rajesh learns about public interest litigation (PIL). A citizen saw children working in brick kilns (child labor). She couldn't afford a lawyer, but filed a PIL in Supreme Court. The Court took it seriously. Ordered: shut down illegal kilns, arrest owners, rehabilitate children. No single person had to suffer—courts intervened for public good. Institutions protect everyone, even the voiceless.

points.label: What is PIL?
points.text: A public-spirited citizen can petition court on behalf of oppressed people. Don't need to be directly harmed. Courts protect public interest.

points.label: Example: Child labor
points.text: A lawyer filed PIL. Supreme Court directed inspections, fines, rehabilitation. Thousands of children freed. All because one person cared enough to petition court.

points.label: Power of courts
points.text: Courts can order executive to act. Can override government decisions. Can protect minorities even against majority wishes. This is judicial independence.

points.label: Access to justice
points.text: Poor people can petition courts (PIL fees are low). Rich can't bribe court into protecting their crimes. Judiciary protects the weak.

slides.inSimpleWords: Courts can act on public interest, even if no individual sues. A concerned citizen petitions court, court orders action. This protects voiceless people.

slides.title: Ombudsman and Grievance Redressal
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's daughter applied for a scholarship. The District Magistrate denied it without reason. She complained to the Lok Pal (Ombudsman). Within weeks, Lok Pal investigated. Found: official made error. Scholarship approved. Ombudsman protects citizens against administrative injustice.

points.label: Lok Pal (National Ombudsman)
points.text: Independent officer who investigates complaints against central government and ministers. Can order action, punish corruption.

points.label: Lok Ayukta (State Ombudsman)
points.text: Similar role for state governments. Appointed by President/Governor on advice of committee.

points.label: What they do
points.text: Investigate corruption, abuse of power, unfair practices. Can summon officials, seize documents. Recommend action. Though enforcement depends on government.

points.label: Citizen's recourse
points.text: If bureaucrat acts unfairly (wrong denial, bribe demand, delay), Ombudsman provides free, informal redressal. No need for costly court case.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ombudsman (Lok Pal) investigates complaints against government officials. Provides free, quick redressal for common citizen grievances.

slides.title: Standing Committees and Parliamentary Oversight
slides.storyContext: Minister Verma explains: 'Parliament has committees. Standing Committee on Finance, Defense, Health, etc. They scrutinize ministry budgets, policies, implementation. More detailed than full Parliament.'

points.label: What is Standing Committee?
points.text: Permanent parliamentary committee. MPs from different parties. Examines specific ministry (Finance, Health, etc.).

points.label: Functions
points.text: Review budget allocation. Scrutinize bills before full debate. Hear ministry officials, experts, affected people. Issue reports with recommendations.

points.label: Teeth
points.text: Committee reports are taken seriously. Ministry must respond. If ignores, Parliament can sanction. Creates pressure for implementation.

points.label: Example
points.text: Standing Committee on Rural Development audits road schemes. Found corruption in Village Roads Project. Recommended prosecution. Action followed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parliamentary committees scrutinize ministries in detail. They review budgets, policies, implementation. Create accountability between question hours.

slides.title: Breaking Down Bureaucratic Walls: Women's Reservation in Government Jobs
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's niece wanted to join police but heard: 'Very few positions for women. Might not clear.' She checked RTI for hiring data. Found: women applicants were rejected without fair evaluation. She filed complaint with Police Commission. They investigated, ordered fair interviews. Now many women are police officers in her district. Institution + citizen action = change.

points.label: Problem
points.text: Gender bias in recruitment. Women were 'discouraged' informally (told they won't clear, won't be respected). Rarely hired.

points.label: RTI revealed
points.text: Hiring data showed: qualified women rejected, underqualified men hired. Pattern of discrimination.

points.label: Redressal
points.text: Police Commission intervened. Ordered transparent interviews, fair evaluation. Removed bias. Result: women recruited.

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Institutions have machinery to fix injustice—RTI to expose, Commission to investigate, courts to punish. Citizens must use them.

slides.inSimpleWords: A woman used RTI to expose gender bias in police hiring. Complaint to Commission led to investigation, and hiring became fair. Institutions worked because citizen demanded it.

slides.title: Delegated Legislation: Ministries Making Rules
slides.storyContext: Minister Verma explains: 'Parliament passes law (bill). But law says, 'Rules will be decided by Ministry.' So Ministry issues Statutory Rules (SR). These are laws too, must be obeyed. But made by bureaucrats, not elected MPs.'

points.label: What is delegated legislation?
points.text: Parliament passes framework law. Gives Ministry power to make detailed rules, implement law. Rules are legally binding.

points.label: Why delegate?
points.text: Parliament debates principles. Ministry handles details (technical matters, procedures, timelines). Too complex for all MPs to decide.

points.label: Example
points.text: Education Act says 'schools must follow curriculum.' Ministry makes detailed curriculum, exam rules. These are delegated legislation.

points.label: Parliamentary oversight
points.text: Parliament can review and reject Ministry's rules (though rare). MPs must ensure delegation isn't abused (doesn't change law's intent).

slides.inSimpleWords: Parliament passes laws. Ministries make detailed rules to implement laws. Rules are laws too, but made by bureaucrats, not elected MPs.

slides.title: Constitutional Amendments: How Parliament Evolves the Constitution
slides.storyContext: Minister Verma explains: 'Sometimes Constitution needs updating. This requires amendment. Need 2/3 Parliamentary majority + (for some parts) state approval. Intentionally difficult, to protect core values.'

points.label: Amendment procedure
points.text: Bill introduced. Debate. Voting. Need 2/3 majority in both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Some amendments need 1/2 states' approval too.

points.label: Why hard?
points.text: Protects Constitution from mob whims. Prevents PM from amending Constitution to seize power. Requires consensus.

points.label: Famous amendments
points.text: 26th Amendment: Lowered voting age from 21 to 18. 44th Amendment (1978): Limited emergency powers. 73rd Amendment: Local government strengthened.

points.label: Basic structure doctrine
points.text: Supreme Court says: some Constitutional features (democracy, secularism, federalism) are so fundamental they can't be amended. Protects Constitution's soul.

slides.inSimpleWords: Constitution amendments need 2/3 Parliamentary majority. Intentionally difficult to prevent misuse. Courts protect Constitution's core values.

slides.title: Transparency: The Right to Information Changes a District
slides.storyContext: Rajesh uses RTI (Right to Information) Act to demand budget records of the District. Discovers: 40% of road funds were siphoned off by corrupt officials! Names and amounts. He files PIL. Court orders investigation. Officials arrested. New tender process is transparent. Villages that were ignored for years get roads. RTI + PIL = accountability. Institutions work when citizens use them.

points.label: RTI opens doors
points.text: Citizens can demand documents—budget, tender bids, inspection reports. Government must provide within 30 days. No more secretive deals.

points.label: Exposing corruption
points.text: RTI revealed that contractors paid kickbacks, got roads built below quality, pocketed difference. RTI made this visible.

points.label: Accountability follows
points.text: Public outcry → media investigation → police FIR → prosecution. Institutions worked in sequence: RTI → courts → enforcement.

points.label: Citizen power
points.text: Rajesh, an ordinary villager, triggered institutional checks against corruption. This is how democracy works—citizens use tools, institutions respond.

slides.inSimpleWords: Right to Information lets citizens demand government documents. Exposed corruption. Led to arrests. Shows citizens can use laws to fix government.

slides.title: What You Learned: How Institutions Work
slides.storyContext: Six months later, Rajesh's bill passes. A road is being built to his village. His daughter starts school in town. Rajesh writes to MP Sharma: 'Thank you. Democracy works. It's slow, but it works.'

points.text: Three-tier government: Central (national laws), State (state issues), Local (villages/towns). Each has separate authority. Federalism.
Parliament (Legislature): Lok Sabha (543 elected) + Rajya Sabha (250 state reps). Makes laws. Holds Executive accountable. Amends Constitution.
Executive (PM & Cabinet): Runs government. Implements laws. Depends on Parliament confidence. Can be removed via no-confidence.
Judiciary (Courts): Interprets laws. Protects rights. Can strike down unconstitutional laws. Independent from politics.
Separation of powers: Each branch checks the others. Prevents power concentration. No single institution dominates.
How a bill becomes law: 6 steps—introduction, first reading, committee review, second reading, third reading, presidential assent. Takes weeks to months.
Accountability: Parliament questions ministers. Courts review laws. Elections remove unpopular leaders. Media exposes corruption.
Democratic slowness: Process is intentionally slow to ensure thorough debate, prevent hasty laws, protect minority concerns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Institutions (Parliament, Executive, Judiciary) divide power and check each other. This prevents tyranny. Laws are debated thoroughly before passing.
